title: Planning and Organising
summary: Planning is the process of setting future objectives and deciding the ways and means of achieving them; it bridges the gap between where we are and where we want to go (M.E. Hurley: deciding in advance what is to be done; selection of objectives, policies, procedures and programmes from alternatives). Features: primary function (precedes organising, staffing, directing and controlling); goal directed; pervasive (all levels and all functional areas: top managers plan for long periods, middle managers quarterly, half-yearly and yearly, supervisors for the next day, week or month); futuristic; an intellectual activity needing foresight and judgement; a continuous process; involves making choices among alternatives; flexible (plans are revised as assumptions change).

Importance: provides direction to action; reduces risk and uncertainty; helps in coordination and facilitates control (basis for controlling by comparing actual with planned results); facilitates decision-making; leads to economy and efficiency in operations. Limitations: rigidity; may not work in a dynamic environment (forecasts can be wrong, e.g. the sub-prime crisis); expensive and time consuming; delay in action; misdirection to serve individual or group interests; creates a false sense of security.

Steps: establishment of objectives; making assumptions (planning premises, external and internal); identifying alternative courses of action; evaluation of alternatives; selecting the course of action (maximum benefit at minimum cost); implementation; review and follow-up. External premises: market demand, competition, laws, resources, technology; internal premises: cost, methods of production, employees, machinery.

Objectives (the end results towards which all activities are directed; measurable, achievable in a time period). Strategy (a comprehensive plan prepared considering competitors' moves for optimum use of resources: Tata's Nano for the middle income group). Policy (a general statement that guides decision-making and sets the boundaries; e.g. training only candidates with more than 60 per cent marks). Procedure (plans determining the sequence of work performance, step by step). Method (determines how one step of the procedure is done; the most efficient uses the least resources). Rule (clearly indicates what is to be done and not to be done; 'No smoking'; strict action on violation). Budget (a statement of expected results in numerical terms: cash budget). Programme (a plan laying down the what, how, who and when of a specific job, with objectives, policies, procedures, budgets: a training programme).

Organising is identifying and grouping activities and bringing together physical, financial and human resources to develop productive relationships among them to achieve objectives. Features: an important function following planning; continuous process; groups activities and defines authority and responsibility; harmonises individual and organisational goals; involves coordination. Authority is the right to command and responsibility the obligation to carry out the work. Importance: leads to specialisation, optimum use of resources, clarity of authority and responsibility, enhances creativity, facilitates expansion and growth, coordination and adaptation to change.

Process of organising: identification of activities; grouping of activities (e.g. purchase, production, marketing, finance); assignment of duties; granting authority; establishing authority-responsibility relationships (coordination). Organisational structure is the framework within which managerial and operating tasks are performed (job specification, departmentalisation, authority-responsibility, span of control). Functional structure (grouping by functions: production, marketing, finance, personnel; specialisation; suitable for small and medium organisations) and divisional structure (separate product divisions, multi-functional; suitable for large organisations with multiple products). Modern structures: team, matrix (project manager and functional manager) and network structures.

Formal organisation: officially established pattern of relationships created by top management to perform jobs systematically; authority from the job position; permanent and stable. Informal organisation: relationships based on personal attitudes, likes and dislikes; arises spontaneously; authority from personal qualities; temporary; supplements the formal organisation and satisfies social and emotional needs.

Delegation is the entrustment of a part of work, responsibility and authority to another and the creation of accountability for performance. Elements: assignment of responsibility (entrustment of duties), granting authority and creating accountability. Importance: reduces managers' workload, improves managerial effectiveness, develops subordinates, builds confidence and motivation and organisational growth. Decentralisation is a systematic effort to delegate authority at all levels of management and in all departments; benefits: reduces top management's workload, motivates employees, promotes initiative, quick decisions and allows top management to concentrate on growth. Delegation is compulsory, narrow in scope (superior and immediate subordinate), undertaken to lessen managers' burden and responsibility is not shared; decentralisation is optional (a policy of top management), wide in scope and involves all levels with shared responsibility.

(i) Organisational structure. (ii) Decentralisation.

Formal organisation: an officially established pattern of relationships created by management with defined authority, rules and procedures, which can be rigid.

Informal organisation; limitation: it can spread rumours and may resist changes.

Is planning probabilistic? Explain.

What is meant by organisational structure?
The framework within which managerial and operating tasks are performed, a network of job positions and authority relationships.

sa: Explain the relationship between planning and controlling.

Planning sets objectives and standards; controlling compares actual results with them and corrects deviations. Planning provides the base for control, and control provides feedback for revising plans: planning looks ahead, controlling looks back.
Explain: (a) Planning is pervasive (b) Planning is a continuous process (c) Planning is futuristic.
(a) Needed at all levels and in all functions. (b) Done again and again as plans are made and revised. (c) Concerned with deciding in advance what to do in the future.
Objectives are end results; strategy is a comprehensive plan considering competitors' moves; policy is a general statement guiding decisions.
Briefly explain: (a) Policy and (b) Rules as types of plans.
A policy is a general guide to decision making within boundaries; a rule clearly states what must or must not be done in a situation, with penalty for violation.
Explain any three importance of planning.
It provides direction, reduces risk and uncertainty and facilitates decision making and control.
Distinguish between formal and informal organisation (three points).
Formal is created by top management, authority from position and permanent; informal arises spontaneously, authority from personal qualities and temporary.
Explain the importance of delegation (three points).
It reduces workload, improves managerial effectiveness and develops subordinates with motivation.
la: Define Centralisation and Decentralisation. Distinguish between them.

Centralisation keeps decision-making authority at top levels; decentralisation systematically delegates authority at all levels. Differences: delegation is compulsory, decentralisation optional; scope narrow versus wide; responsibility shared in decentralisation only; purpose to lessen burden versus to increase subordinates' role.
April 2026
'Planning is looking ahead, Controlling is looking back.' Analyse and explain the statement.

Planning decides in advance objectives and ways of achieving them; controlling compares actual results with plans and takes corrective action after performance; both are interdependent: planning provides standards, controlling provides feedback.
April 2026

Establishing objectives, making assumptions (premises), identifying alternatives, evaluating alternatives, selecting a course of action, implementing the plan, and review and follow-up.
April 2025
Explain the process of organising.
Identification of activities, grouping them into departments, assignment of duties, granting authority and establishing authority-responsibility relationships for coordination.
April 2025
What is meant by delegation? Briefly explain its elements.
Delegation is entrusting work and authority to another with accountability; elements: assignment of responsibility, granting authority and creating accountability.
October 2024
Briefly explain any five points of importance of planning.
Gives direction, reduces risk and uncertainty, coordination, facilitates decision-making, economy and efficiency and control.

It leads to specialisation, optimum use of resources, clarity of authority, creativity, growth, coordination and adaptation to change.
